# JSON Schema

> Convert Types to JSON Schema and back

# Overview

> Generate JSON Schema from a Type with arktype, or build a Type from JSON Schema with @ark/json-schema.

ArkType converts in both directions, with one package for each.

| direction | package | API |
| - | - | - |
| Type → JSON Schema | `arktype` | `T.toJsonSchema()`, `T["~standard"].jsonSchema` |
| JSON Schema → Type | `@ark/json-schema` | `jsonSchemaToType(schema)` |

## Type to JSON Schema

Every Type has a `toJsonSchema()` method. Nothing else to install:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

const schema = User.toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"name": { "type": "string" },
		"age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
	},
	"required": ["name"]
}
```

Some things a Type can check, like a `Date`, a `bigint` or a custom `narrow`, have no JSON Schema equivalent. `toJsonSchema()` throws on those unless you tell it what to write instead. See [To JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema).

Libraries that accept any [Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema) read it from `T["~standard"].jsonSchema`, which never throws for those parts. See [Standard JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#standard-json-schema).

## JSON Schema to Type

`@ark/json-schema` parses a JSON Schema into a Type:

```bash
npm install @ark/json-schema
```

```ts
import { jsonSchemaToType } from "@ark/json-schema"

const User = jsonSchemaToType({
	type: "object",
	properties: {
		name: { type: "string" },
		age: { type: "integer", minimum: 0 }
	},
	required: ["name"]
})

User.expression // "{ name: string, age?: number % 1 >= 0 }"
// ArkErrors: age must be an integer (was 1.5)
User({ name: "Ada", age: 1.5 })
```

A schema written in the call infers its type, so `User` is a `Type<{ name: string; age?: number }>`. See [From JSON Schema](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema#inferring-its-type) to type a schema declared elsewhere, and [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) for which keywords it understands.

# To JSON Schema

> Generate a JSON Schema from any Type, pick a draft, and decide what to write for what JSON Schema can't express.

Every Type has a `toJsonSchema()` method:

```ts
const User = type({
	name: "string",
	"age?": "number.integer >= 0"
})

const schema = User.toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"name": { "type": "string" },
		"age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }
	},
	"required": ["name"]
}
```

A [precompiled](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile) validator has `toJsonSchema()`, its schema baked at build time, where its build sees code call it or its [`members`](https://arktype.io/docs/precompile/options#members) option sets it.

## Options

| option | default | effect |
| - | - | - |
| `target` | `"draft-2020-12"` | what to write, `"draft-2020-12"`, `"draft-07"` or [`"openapi-3.0"`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#openapi-30) |
| `dialect` | the target's URL | the `$schema` value. `null` omits it. Takes precedence over `target`'s URL |
| `useRefs` | `false` | write every part once under `$defs`, not only [cyclic aliases](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#cyclic-types), and point to it with `$ref` |
| `fallback` | throws | what to write for a part JSON Schema can't express. See [Fallbacks](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallbacks) |

### target

The drafts differ in how they write tuples and where they put definitions:

```ts
const Pair = type(["string", "number"])

Pair.toJsonSchema()
// {
// 	$schema: "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
// 	type: "array",
// 	minItems: 2,
// 	prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }],
// 	items: false
// }

Pair.toJsonSchema({ target: "draft-07" })
// {
// 	$schema: "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
// 	type: "array",
// 	minItems: 2,
// 	items: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }],
// 	additionalItems: false
// }
```

`draft-07` writes `definitions` where `draft-2020-12` writes `$defs`.

### OpenAPI 3.0

`"openapi-3.0"` writes an [OpenAPI 3.0 Schema Object](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.0.3#schema-object), which has no `$schema` and words some keywords differently:

| draft 2020-12 | `"openapi-3.0"` |
| - | - |
| `exclusiveMinimum: 0` | `minimum: 0`, `exclusiveMinimum: true` |
| `type: "string"`, `const: "cat"` | `type: "string"`, `enum: ["cat"]` |
| `not: { const: 5 }` | `not: { enum: [5] }` |
| `anyOf: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "null" }]` | `type: "string"`, `nullable: true` |
| `type: "null"` | `type: "string"`, `nullable: true`, `enum: [null]` |
| `examples: ["a", "b"]` | `example: "a"` |
| `contentEncoding: "base64"` | `format: "byte"` |
| `type: "array"` | `type: "array"`, `items: {}` |

`nullable` adds `null` only to the `type` beside it, and an `enum` there must list `null` too. A union whose other branches share no `type`, like `string | number | null`, keeps `null` as a branch of its `anyOf`. OpenAPI 3.0 has no `null` type, so `null` alone is written as zod writes it: a `nullable` string whose `enum` allows only `null`.

What OpenAPI 3.0 can't express goes to a [fallback](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallbacks), so `toJsonSchema()` throws for it by default:

- A tuple's elements, since `items` is one schema for every element, go to `arrayPrefix`.
- `patternProperties` and `propertyNames` go to `indexKey`. A `string` index signature with no declared keys is still `additionalProperties`.
- Definitions go to `defs`. A `$ref` points into the document's `#/components/schemas`, which a Schema Object can't hold, so the handler receives them to put there:

```ts
import { scope, type JsonSchema } from "arktype"

const types = scope({ Node: { value: "number", "next?": "Node" } }).export()

const components: Record<string, JsonSchema> = {}

// { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Node" }
const schema = types.Node.toJsonSchema({
	target: "openapi-3.0",
	fallback: {
		defs: ctx => {
			// { Node: { type: "object", properties: { ... } } }
			Object.assign(components, ctx.defs)
			return ctx.base
		}
	}
})
```

zod, valibot and sury write a tuple as an array whose elements may each be any of its elements, which accepts `[1, "a"]` for `["string", "number"]`. To write it that way:

```ts
const Pair = type(["string", "number"])

// {
// 	type: "array",
// 	items: { anyOf: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }] },
// 	minItems: 2,
// 	maxItems: 2
// }
Pair.toJsonSchema({
	target: "openapi-3.0",
	fallback: {
		arrayPrefix: ({ base, elements, items }) => ({
			...base,
			items: { anyOf: items ? [...elements, items] : elements }
		})
	}
})
```

[`jsonSchema` meta](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#your-own-schema) is written as configured, so `string.json`'s `contentMediaType`, which OpenAPI 3.0 lacks, is too.

### dialect

```ts
type("string").toJsonSchema({ dialect: null }) // { type: "string" }
```

### Cyclic types

A cyclic alias is written once under `$defs`, named by its alias, and each reference to it is a `$ref`. Everything else, including an alias that isn't cyclic, is written inline:

```ts
const types = scope({ Node: { value: "number", "next?": "Node" } }).export()

const schema = types.Node.toJsonSchema()
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"$ref": "#/$defs/Node",
	"$defs": {
		"Node": {
			"type": "object",
			"properties": {
				"value": { "type": "number" },
				"next": { "$ref": "#/$defs/Node" }
			},
			"required": ["value"]
		}
	}
}
```

- A generic's instantiations are named by the generic, like `Box` for `Box<string>`, and a submodule's alias by its own name, like `B` for `A.B`.
- A name another definition already has is numbered from 2, like `Node2`, in the order the definitions are reached.
- A cycle with no alias, like a `this` reference, is named by what ArkType calls it, like `type`.
- `.in`, `.out` and `~standard.jsonSchema` name definitions the same way.

## How Types map

| ArkType | JSON Schema |
| - | - |
| `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"null"` | `type` |
| `"number.integer"`, `"number % 2"` | `type: "integer"`, plus `multipleOf: 2` |
| `"0 < number <= 1"` | `exclusiveMinimum: 0`, `maximum: 1` |
| `"string >= 1"`, `"string == 2"` | `minLength`, or `minLength` and `maxLength` |
| `"string[] > 0"` | `items`, `minItems: 1` |
| `["string", "number?"]` | `prefixItems`, `minItems: 1`, `items: false` |
| `/^a/` | `pattern: "^a"` |
| `"string.email"`, `"string.uuid"` | `pattern`, `format: "email"`, `"uuid"` |
| `"string.ip.v4"`, `"string.ip.v6"` | `pattern`, `format: "ipv4"`, `"ipv6"` |
| `"string.date.iso"` | `pattern`, `format: "date-time"` |
| `"string.base64"` | `pattern`, `contentEncoding: "base64"` |
| `"string.base64.url"` | `pattern`, `contentEncoding: "base64url"` |
| `"string.date"`, `"string.url"`, `"string.regex"` | `format: "date-time"`, `"uri"`, `"regex"` |
| `"string.json"` | `contentMediaType: "application/json"` |
| `"'a' \| 'b'"` | `type: "string"`, `enum: ["a", "b"]` |
| `"string \| null"` | `anyOf` |
| `{ "name?": "string" }` | `properties`, with only required keys in `required` |
| `{ "+": "reject", ... }` | `additionalProperties: false` |
| `"Record<string, number>"` | `additionalProperties: {...}` |
| `{ id: "string", "[string]": "string" }` | `patternProperties: { "": {...} }` |
| `{ "[/^x-/]": "string" }` | `patternProperties: { "^x-": {...} }` |
| `{ "[string <= 3]": "number", "+": "reject" }` | `propertyNames`, `additionalProperties: {...}` |
| `{ role: "string = 'user'" }` | `default: "user"` on `role` |
| `.describe("...")`, `.configure({ title, examples })` | `description`, `title`, `examples` |

JSON Schema's `pattern` has no flags. `d` and `g` don't change what a regex matches, so they're left out, as is `u` for draft 2020-12, whose patterns are read with it. Any other flag, like `i` in `/^a/i`, goes to the [`patternFlags`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) fallback.

An index signature applies to every key, including declared ones. JSON Schema skips declared keys in `additionalProperties`, so an index signature next to declared keys is written as `patternProperties` with a pattern every key matches.

A keyword's `format`, `contentEncoding` or `contentMediaType` names what its strings are. JSON Schema reads each as an annotation, which a validator doesn't check unless it's configured to, so it's written whether or not arktype's check matches the standard's definition exactly. A keyword checked by a regex is written with that `pattern` too, so a validator that ignores formats still checks what arktype does. One checked by a function is written as its format alone: `string.date` accepts whatever `Date` parses, and `string.url` whatever `URL.canParse` does, so their schemas accept strings the Type rejects. A validator that asserts formats, like Ajv with `ajv-formats`, can also reject strings arktype accepts, where a format's RFC differs from arktype's check: `date-time` requires a time that `string.date` and `string.date.iso` don't, and `uri` rejects the space in a path that `string.url` accepts. Keywords no format names, like `string.date.epoch` or `string.creditCard`, go to the [`predicate`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) fallback.

A key that isn't `string` or a single regex, like `[string <= 3]`, needs `propertyNames`, which checks every key of the object. That's only the same thing when every key must match it: undeclared keys are rejected, it's the only index signature, and every declared key matches it. Any other such key goes to the [`indexKey`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) fallback.

## Your own schema

Configure `jsonSchema` meta to write a Type's schema yourself. It replaces the schema the Type's constraints imply, so a `narrow` it covers needs no fallback:

```ts
const Even = type("number")
	.narrow(n => n % 2 === 0)
	.configure({ jsonSchema: { type: "integer", multipleOf: 2 } })

Even.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", type: "integer", multipleOf: 2 }
```

The Type's other meta, like a description, is still written beside it. Unlike other meta, `jsonSchema` is configured on the Type alone, not on the Types it references, since it describes the whole Type.

## Fallbacks

Some things a Type checks have no JSON Schema equivalent: a `Date`, a `bigint`, a morph, a `narrow`. By default, `toJsonSchema()` throws a `ToJsonSchemaError` for them, naming where it is and which fallback to configure:

```ts
type({ at: "Date" }).toJsonSchema() // throws ToJsonSchemaError (code "date")
```

Pass a handler for its [code](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) to write something instead. The handler receives the schema written so far as `ctx.base`, plus fields for its code, and returns the schema to use:

```ts
const Event = type({ name: "string", at: "Date" })

const schema = Event.toJsonSchema({
	fallback: {
		date: ctx => ({ ...ctx.base, type: "string", format: "date-time" })
	}
})
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"at": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" },
		"name": { "type": "string" }
	},
	"required": ["at", "name"]
}
```

A `default` handler covers every code you don't list. Passing a function instead of an object is the same as passing it as `default`. Return `ctx.base` to leave out what JSON Schema can't express:

```ts
// properties.at is now {}
Event.toJsonSchema({ fallback: ctx => ctx.base })
```

Leaving something out makes the schema accept values the Type rejects.

For `defaultValue`, `base` is the property's own schema, so returning it makes the schema contain itself. Return `undefined` to drop the default instead, e.g. `{ defaultValue: () => undefined, default: ctx => ctx.base }`.

### Morphs

A morph has a different input and output, so there is no single schema for it. Convert one side with `.in` or `.out`:

```ts
const Tags = type("string")
	.pipe(s => s.split(","))
	.to("string[]")

Tags.in.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", type: "string" }
Tags.out.toJsonSchema() // { $schema: "...", type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }
```

### annotatingFallback

To keep what JSON Schema can't express rather than drop it, pass `annotatingFallback`. It writes each such constraint as an `x-arktype-*` keyword, naming a function, class or symbol by its `$ark` name as a Type's `.json` does:

```ts
import { annotatingFallback, type } from "arktype"

const schema = type({
	id: "bigint",
	createdAt: "Date"
}).toJsonSchema({ fallback: annotatingFallback })
```

```json
{
	"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
	"type": "object",
	"properties": {
		"createdAt": { "x-arktype-proto": "Date" },
		"id": { "x-arktype-domain": "bigint" }
	},
	"required": ["createdAt", "id"]
}
```

Validators ignore those keywords, so the schema still accepts values the Type rejects.

### Fallback codes

Every reason `toJsonSchema()` can throw, with the fields its handler receives besides `code` and `base`:

| code | raised for | example | fields |
| - | - | - | - |
| `arrayObject` | an array with named properties | `type("string[]").and({ n: "number" })` | `object` |
| `arrayPostfix` | elements after a variadic element | `type(["...", "string[]", "number"])` | `elements` |
| `arrayPrefix` | for `openapi-3.0`, elements before any variadic element | `type(["string", "number"])` | `elements`, and `items` for the rest, if any |
| `date` | a `Date`, with its bounds | `type("Date")` | `before`, `after` |
| `defaultValue` | a default that isn't JSON. Return `undefined` to omit it | `type({ n: "bigint = 5n" })`, after `domain` | `value` |
| `defs` | for `openapi-3.0`, the definitions `$ref`s point to | a cyclic Type | `defs`, by name |
| `domain` | `bigint` or `symbol` | `type("bigint")` | `domain` |
| `indexKey` | a key `propertyNames` can't express, or for `openapi-3.0` any key but a lone `string` | `type({ "[string <= 3]": "number" })` | `key` and `value`, as schemas |
| `morph` | a morph | `type("string.trim")` | `out`, the output schema or `null` |
| `patternFlags` | a regex flag other than `d`, `g` or, for draft 2020-12, `u` | `type(/^a/i)` | `pattern`, `flags` |
| `patternIntersection` | a second regex on the same string | `type(/^a/).and(/b$/)` | `pattern` |
| `predicate` | a `narrow`, or `object.json`'s plain-object check | `type("number").narrow(n => n > 0)` | `predicate` |
| `proto` | an `instanceof` other than `Array` or `Date` | `type("Map")` | `proto` |
| `symbolKey` | a symbol key or index signature | `type({ "[symbol]": "string" })` | `key` (`null` for an index), `value`, `optional` |
| `unit` | a literal that isn't JSON | `type("undefined")` | `unit` |

A `Date` is reported as `date`, never `proto`.

`object.json` accepts only arrays and objects whose prototype is `Object.prototype` or `null`, which JSON Schema can't require, so its check is reported as `predicate`. Return `ctx.base` to accept any JSON object in its place:

```ts
// { type: "object", additionalProperties: { $ref: "#/$defs/jsonData" }, $defs: { jsonData: { anyOf: [...] } } }
type("object.json").toJsonSchema({ fallback: { predicate: ctx => ctx.base } })
```

## Configuration

`toJsonSchema` options can also be set [globally or on a scope](https://arktype.io/docs/configuration#levels). Options passed to `toJsonSchema()` are merged over them:

```ts
import { configure } from "arktype/config"

configure({
	toJsonSchema: {
		target: "draft-07",
		fallback: {
			date: ctx => ({ ...ctx.base, type: "string", format: "date-time" })
		}
	}
})
```

```ts
// import your config file before arktype
import "./config.ts"
import { type } from "arktype"

// $schema is draft-07's, and at is { type: "string", format: "date-time" }
type({ at: "Date" }).toJsonSchema()
```

A handler passed to `toJsonSchema()` replaces the configured one for its code. A `default` passed there replaces every configured handler.

## Standard JSON Schema

Libraries that accept any [Standard JSON Schema](https://standardschema.dev/json-schema) read a Type's schema from `~standard.jsonSchema`. `input` describes what the Type accepts, `output` what it returns after its morphs:

```ts
const Form = type({
	tags: type("string")
		.pipe(s => s.split(","))
		.to("string[]"),
	"id?": "bigint"
})

// properties: { tags: { type: "string" }, id: {} }
Form["~standard"].jsonSchema.input({ target: "draft-2020-12" })

// properties: { tags: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }, id: {} }
Form["~standard"].jsonSchema.output({ target: "draft-2020-12" })
```

Unlike `toJsonSchema()`, these never throw for a part JSON Schema can't express. They write as much of it as JSON Schema can describe, or `{}` if nothing, so `id` above accepts any value. A regex with flags is left out too, and so is an index signature `propertyNames` can't express, along with the `additionalProperties: false` that would reject the keys it allows.

- `target` must be `"draft-2020-12"`, `"draft-07"` or `"openapi-3.0"`. Anything else throws.
- For `"openapi-3.0"`, a tuple is an array of its length, and definitions are written beside the `$ref` as `definitions`, for you to move into `#/components/schemas`, where the `$ref`s point.
- `libraryOptions` are passed to `toJsonSchema()` as options, e.g. `{ dialect: null }`.
- Fallback handlers you configure or pass in `libraryOptions` still apply. Only the default throwing handlers are replaced.
- `input` writes each morph's input, so it never calls a `morph` handler. It keeps defaults, and allows keys `"+": "delete"` would remove.

# From JSON Schema

> Parse a JSON Schema into a Type with @ark/json-schema and give the result a static type.

```bash
npm install @ark/json-schema
```

`arktype` is a peer dependency of `@ark/json-schema`, at the version released with it, so the Types it returns come from your own `arktype`. Install the versions released together; with any other, npm refuses the install and pnpm warns.

`jsonSchemaToType` parses a JSON Schema into a Type:

```ts
import { jsonSchemaToType } from "@ark/json-schema"

const User = jsonSchemaToType({
	type: "object",
	properties: {
		name: { type: "string" },
		age: { type: "integer", minimum: 0 }
	},
	required: ["name"]
})

User.expression // "{ name: string, age?: number % 1 >= 0 }"
User({ name: "Ada" }) // { name: "Ada" }
// ArkErrors: age must be an integer (was 1.5)
User({ name: "Ada", age: 1.5 })
```

`true` parses to `unknown` and `false` to `never`.

## Inferring its type

`jsonSchemaToType` infers the type of a schema written in the call:

```ts
import { jsonSchemaToType } from "@ark/json-schema"

const User = jsonSchemaToType({
	type: "object",
	properties: {
		name: { type: "string" },
		tags: { type: "array", items: { type: "string" } }
	},
	required: ["name"]
})

// { name: string; tags?: string[] }
type User = typeof User.infer
```

The inferred type never rejects a value the schema accepts, but it can be wider: constraints like `minimum` and `pattern` don't narrow it, and a `$ref` that isn't a JSON Pointer, like one to an anchor, infers `unknown`. Inference follows `$ref`s into `$defs`, `definitions` and OpenAPI `components.schemas`, including recursive ones, and composition, `if`/`then`/`else` and `not`.

To check and infer a schema you declare apart from the call, wrap it in `jsonSchema`, which returns it unchanged:

```ts
import { jsonSchema, jsonSchemaToType } from "@ark/json-schema"

const Address = jsonSchema({
	type: "object",
	properties: { city: { type: "string" }, zip: { type: "string" } },
	required: ["city"]
})

// { city: string; zip?: string }
type Address = typeof Address.infer

// Type<{ city: string; zip?: string }>
const T = jsonSchemaToType(Address)
```

A schema TypeScript can't see as a literal, like one parsed from a `.json` file, infers `unknown`. If you know its shape, cast it with `jsonSchema.as`:

```ts
const User = jsonSchemaToType(jsonSchema.as<{ name: string }>(userJson))

// { name: string }
const user = User.assert({ name: "Ada" })
```

`jsonSchema.as` is not checked against the schema, so keep the two in sync yourself. To write your own wrapper, `jsonSchema.validate<schema>` checks a schema and `jsonSchema.infer<schema>` infers it.

## How it reads JSON Schema

`jsonSchemaToType` reads a schema with [`arksets`](https://arktype.io/docs/sets)' `parse`, so the Type accepts exactly what a JSON Schema 2020-12 validator accepts, except that lengths count UTF-16 code units, with ajv as the tiebreaker. Every keyword in a schema applies, local `$ref`s resolve, including recursive ones, and draft-07 forms like `items` arrays and `definitions` are read too:

```ts
import { jsonSchemaToType } from "@ark/json-schema"

const Tree = jsonSchemaToType({
	$defs: {
		Node: {
			type: "object",
			properties: {
				value: { type: "number" },
				children: { type: "array", items: { $ref: "#/$defs/Node" } }
			},
			required: ["value"]
		}
	},
	$ref: "#/$defs/Node"
})

Tree.allows({ value: 1, children: [{ value: 2 }] }) // true
```

[Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) lists how each keyword is read.

## Invalid schemas

A schema written in the call, or in `jsonSchema`, is checked as you write it:

```ts
// TypeScript: minLength must be a non-negative integer (was -1)
jsonSchemaToType({ type: "string", minLength: -1 })

// TypeScript: unevaluatedProperties isn't supported by jsonSchemaToType
jsonSchemaToType({ type: "object", unevaluatedProperties: false })
```

`jsonSchemaToType` throws a `ParseError` naming the keyword's JSON Pointer for an invalid keyword TypeScript can't check, like a `pattern`, or one it can't read exactly, like a `$ref` to another document:

```ts
// ParseError: #/pattern must be a valid pattern (was "[")
jsonSchemaToType({ type: "string", pattern: "[" })

// ParseError: #/$ref must reference a schema in its own document (was https://example.com/user.json)
jsonSchemaToType({ $ref: "https://example.com/user.json" })
```

Of the keywords it can't read, `$dynamicRef`, `$recursiveRef`, `unevaluatedItems`, `unevaluatedProperties` and a draft-04 boolean `exclusiveMinimum` or `exclusiveMaximum` are type errors too.

One check is deliberately stricter than JSON Schema: a `required` key a schema's own `properties` don't declare is a type error where nothing else could declare it. That's a schema with no `patternProperties`, composition keyword, `$ref` or dependent schema, whose `additionalProperties` is absent or `false`, reached from the root only through the `properties`, `additionalProperties`, `items` or `prefixItems` of schemas like it. JSON Schema reads the key as required with any value, but it's usually a typo.

## Typing a schema

To check a schema you declare separately without inferring it, use `JsonSchema` from `arktype`:

```ts
import type { JsonSchema } from "arktype"

const Age = {
	type: "integer",
	minimum: 0
} satisfies JsonSchema.Numeric
```

For a string schema, `StringSchema` from `@ark/json-schema` matches what `jsonSchemaToType` reads more closely than `JsonSchema.String`: it leaves out `format`, which isn't validated, and its `pattern` can be a `RegExp`, read with its own flags:

```ts
import type { StringSchema } from "@ark/json-schema"

const Slug = {
	type: "string",
	pattern: /^[a-z-]+$/,
	maxLength: 64
} satisfies StringSchema
```

## JsonSchemaScope

`JsonSchemaScope` is a [module](https://arktype.io/docs/scopes) whose `ArraySchema`, `NumberSchema`, `ObjectSchema` and `StringSchema` Types check a schema of that kind without converting it:

```ts
import { JsonSchemaScope } from "@ark/json-schema"

// ArkErrors: minimum must be a number (was a string)
JsonSchemaScope.NumberSchema({ type: "number", minimum: "0" })
```

## Back to JSON Schema

A Type from `jsonSchemaToType` has [`toJsonSchema()`](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema) like any other. Keywords [Keyword support](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/support) lists as opaque, like `uniqueItems`, `not` and `if`, come back as [`predicate` fallbacks](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes), so `toJsonSchema()` throws for them unless you handle that code.

To normalize one JSON Schema into another, or to compare JSON Schemas with each other and with Types from other libraries, use [ArkSets](https://arktype.io/docs/sets).

# Keyword support

> How @ark/json-schema and arksets read each JSON Schema keyword, which ones throw, and which are only annotations.

`jsonSchemaToType` and [ArkSets](https://arktype.io/docs/sets) read JSON Schema the same way. A Type read from a schema accepts exactly what a JSON Schema 2020-12 validator accepts, except that lengths count UTF-16 code units, with ajv as the tiebreaker. Each keyword is read in one of five ways:

- **supported**: the Type checks it, and [relations](https://arktype.io/docs/sets/relations) like `isSubset` reason about it.
- **opaque**: the Type checks it exactly, with a predicate. Relations through it can't be proven, and `toJsonSchema()` needs a [`predicate` fallback](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/to-json-schema#fallback-codes) to write it back.
- **annotation**: kept as the Type's metadata, and not validated.
- **throws**: reading the schema throws a `ParseError` naming the keyword's JSON Pointer.
- **ignored**: has no effect.

Every keyword in a schema applies, and a type's keywords constrain only that type, as JSON Schema says: `{ minimum: 5 }` accepts `"foo"`, and `{ type: ["string", "number"], minLength: 2 }` accepts `3` but not `"a"`.

A keyword with an invalid value throws, like `#/minLength must be a non-negative integer (was -1)`. A keyword JSON Schema doesn't define is ignored.

OpenAPI 3.0's own forms, which `toJsonSchema({ target: "openapi-3.0" })` writes, aren't read: `nullable` and `example` are ignored, and a boolean `exclusiveMinimum` throws.

`jsonSchemaToType` checks a schema written in the call as you write it: an invalid keyword value is a type error, as is each keyword below that throws, except a `$ref` to another document. See [Invalid schemas](https://arktype.io/docs/json-schema/from-json-schema#invalid-schemas).

## Core

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `true`, `false` | supported | `unknown` and `never` |
| `type` | supported | a name or an array of names. `"object"` excludes arrays |
| `const`, `enum` | supported | objects and arrays are compared by value |
| `$ref` | supported | `#`, a JSON Pointer like `#/$defs/Node`, an anchor or an embedded `$id`, including recursive refs |
| `$ref` to another document | **throws** | only refs into the same document are resolved |
| `$defs`, `definitions` | supported | read where a `$ref` points to them |
| `$dynamicRef`, `$recursiveRef` | **throws** | |
| `title`, `description`, `default`, `examples`, `deprecated` | annotation | `default` is not applied |
| `$schema` | annotation | draft-07 or earlier ignores the keywords beside a `$ref`, as those drafts do |
| `$id`, `$anchor`, `$dynamicAnchor` | supported | identify a schema a `$ref` resolves to. Draft-04 reads `id` |
| `$comment`, `readOnly`, `writeOnly` | **ignored** | |
| `contentEncoding`, `contentMediaType` | **ignored** | annotations in 2020-12 |
| `nullable` (OpenAPI 3.0) | **ignored** | write `type: ["string", "null"]` instead |

## Composition

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `allOf`, `anyOf` | supported | |
| `oneOf` | supported | when its branches are disjoint, it's a union. Otherwise, opaque |
| `not` | opaque | |
| `if`, `then`, `else` | opaque | `if` without `then` or `else` has no effect |

Composition keywords apply together and beside any other keyword:

```ts
import { jsonSchemaToType } from "@ark/json-schema"

const T = jsonSchemaToType({
	anyOf: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }],
	not: { const: 0 }
})

T.allows("a") // true
// ArkErrors: must be other than 0 (was 0)
T(0)
```

## Strings

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `minLength`, `maxLength` | supported | counts UTF-16 code units, as arktype's bounds do, where JSON Schema counts code points |
| `pattern` | supported | a string, or a `RegExp` read with its own flags |
| `format` | annotation | as the spec defaults to, and as `toJsonSchema()` writes it |

## Numbers

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `minimum`, `maximum` | supported | |
| `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum` | supported | a number. Draft 4's boolean form throws |
| `multipleOf` | supported | an integer. Any other positive number, opaque |

## Arrays

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `prefixItems`, `items` | supported | prefix elements are optional, as JSON Schema says: `[string?, number?, ...unknown[]]`. `items` is the rest |
| `items` as an array, `additionalItems` | supported | draft-07's tuples |
| `minItems`, `maxItems` | supported | |
| `uniqueItems` | opaque | items are compared as JSON values |
| `contains`, `minContains`, `maxContains` | opaque | |
| `unevaluatedItems` | **throws** | |

## Objects

| keyword | support | notes |
| - | - | - |
| `properties`, `required` | supported | a `required` key not in `properties` must be present, with any value |
| `patternProperties` | supported | |
| `additionalProperties` | supported | `false` rejects other keys. A schema is an index signature alone, or opaque beside `properties` |
| `propertyNames`, `minProperties`, `maxProperties` | opaque | |
| `dependentRequired`, `dependentSchemas`, `dependencies` | opaque | |
| `unevaluatedProperties` | **throws** | |
